commentBody: Nice long acrosses and center stack. Pitched just right for Sunday

My Saturday, my Sunday.
My Saturday, my Sunday.
My Saturday and my Sunday.

Forget it, Jake: It's Crosswordtown.

I have to endure the complaints every time there's a rebus from people who have no idea that rebuses have been a thing since 1954.

Themeless Sundays have only been a thing for a few years, and they only appear a couple of times in a year.  Someone apparently though back then that they would be a good idea.

But I'm quite disappointed when I realize that it is one.  (And that's fairly early on, based on the grid shape--no obvious theme answers--and the title, which always conveys in apparently endless ways, that there's no "there" there.)

I do them, because I do all of them, but I don't have to like them.

Why don't I like them?  Because at the size of a Sunday puzzle, the lack of a theme makes the puzzle boring, it drags on, and it lacks humor.  This particular puzzle was no different.

At least it'll be six months before the next one.
There are some puzzle creators you are just simpatico with. I always enjoy an Eric Asgard construction.
Leiden jar or LEYDEN jar??

What a gorgeous grid, stagger stacks in the middle, abutting spanners above and below.  The typical Sunday grid has 74 blocks and 139 words, and this one has 58 blocks and 128 words.  You’d expect a presence of ugly fill in such a low-count grid – but not if it were made by Erik.  His grids are unfailingly clean.

And even with the difficulty of filling a low count grid, Erik put in a dozen NYT answer debuts for spark, my favorite two being ALPHABET SONG (with its world-class clue) and COME ON IN THE WATER’S FINE.

Everything flows in this grid – no scary islands to fill in.  Even that huge tablet-shaped area in the middle is entered by four long answers.

Plenty of answers and clues to love; I never felt bored.  A shining, sterling, fun-to-solve beauty, which is the rule of your puzzles, Erik.  Nothing but quality in them.  Thank you, and please, keep creating!

What a lovely puzzle! Really enjoyed it, and learned a few things, too. :)

Wow. That was a challenge for me. ISOLDE/SALAT, the fact that DIDRIKSON fit the female baseball player clue and DECLINING over DIVESTING held me up extensively, especially throughout the middle section, where I struggled to get a foothold. 

But an impressive construction nonetheless with so few clues.

Some complain about Sunday puzzles with no theme. I say a Sunday doesn't need a theme when it's as well crafted as this one.

I got my initial toehold in the middle right section and largely proceeded clockwise from there.

I know Sunday themeless puzzles are controversial and I’m sure this will be no different. I don’t mind them on occasion but if so they need to be really amazing. And this one was really amazing. What else would you expect from Erik Agard?

That center was absolutely brilliant, I can’t even imagine how hard it was to fill that. And some great clues—Sam’s “Honey Boo Boo” is an instant classic, and the clue for MOLASSES and ALPHABET SONG aren’t far behind. The NEUROLOGY clue was pretty brainy too.

I also loved the look of the grid, that center looked a bit like a swimming pool (or maybe a skating rink).

Minor nit—maybe it’s not completely against the rules but I didn’t like SWAM crossing an entry with the word “swimmer” in the clue. (I like the entries, especially in a puzzle called “Freestyle”, I just wish 19 across was clued a bit differently.

Mario haters did last week at least prime you for WARIO today?

Listen, no shade if you didn’t like this or thought it was a slog, I get it. Just count me as a fan, personally.

Then all the proper noun/trivia answers like TONI STONE, ISOLDE, SILENTA, SALAT, MAVEN, COVEY, MOORE, NLRB.  Just so many "Know it or you don't" answers that all converged in the same region.  Very frustrating puzzle.

I enjoyed the puzzle, although I got tripped up in the SE corner. 

One nitpick with the NYT column: As a rollercoaster enthusiast (“thoosie”), the photo of Outlaw Run at Silver Dollar City does not depict an “inverted coaster” although that coaster does have inversions. An “inverted coaster” hangs below the track, like the Batman rides at many Six Flags parks.

Wait! This was themeless? When I read the title "Freestyle Exercise," I straightaway thought of swimming--specifically doing the (Australian) crawl. This was reaffirmed with the grid art, the center of which looks to me like it could be a swimming pool, perhaps one designed for water polo, with two goal nets at either end. Of course, this was clearly the case--with watery entries like SWAM, OCEANUS, SWAMP, and of course COMEONINTHEWATERSFINE. And there it ended. But it gave me a good excuse to look up YouTubes of Michael Nyman's *Water Dances*: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=5Zp44v3rRvU&list=RD5Zp44v3rRvU&start_radio=1 (What's Michael doing at 0:17--trying to shake some pool water out of his ear?) 80's pop minimalism not to your taste? Here's the Roches' tribute to 38D, 43D, 47D, 62A, and 66A: https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=3QMApfa5AUo&list=RD3QMApfa5AUo&start_radio=1

I got a little disappointed the last couple times I encountered a themeless Sunday. I generally enjoy most of the themes in the crosswords, so 'twas disappointing to not get one. 

Today was an exception for me. I really enjoyed it this one, even though there was no theme. I enjoyed a number of fresh seeming entries, especially the crossing swimming entries, the bee sting clue, learning about Toni Stone, and the thought of peace at 1A.

The freestyle title and the early on swimming clues, plus the grid shape, at first made me think it was going to be some kind of swimming theme, but I was quickly disabused of that notion when I couldn't see any seeming connection between long answers, plus no revealer (not that all things have revealers).

Anyhow, I thought it was a lot of fun and before I knew it, I was done, a fair bit faster than I expected to be. But, and here is where I'm going to dismay two different fandoms... 

At 34 down, discovered only upon flyspecking after I didn't get the happy music, I had entered LETITgo....  😂😂😂

Actually, probably have enraged three fandoms, now that I think of it. 

Sorry all you Beatles, Frozen, and James Bond fans!! I have let you all down!! I hope you will choose to either let it go, let it be, or shake me up a martini so that we may move forward in peace. 

☮️🍸❤️

Oh shoot, I offended all the unions too... My apologies!!

I have never heard the expression "have things out". I've heard "have it out", but that is an idiom, and an idiom is a lexical unit - you can't just change words and have the same meaning. You wouldn't say, "he kicked a bucket", or "beat around the shrub".

I used to not care about themes.  Couldn't even really understand what all the fuss was about.  Apparently, I have joined Team Theme, because as I realized this didn't have one, I felt a little let down.  I've come to look forward to figuring them out, and often, the humor they supply.  In a big Sunday grid, they provide momentum and keep things from getting tedious.

But...

This is Eric Agard!  

He can do no wrong in my book.  This was so filled with fresh entries, and I liked all of the long spanners.  

Well, most of them anyway.  COME IN THE WATERS FINE crossing SWAM felt like a poke in the eye here at day 9 of a cyanobacteria outbreak in my neighborhood pond.  And yes, that sad POOL at 86 A is where you'll find me until things clear up.

Love that crazy ellipse at the center of the grid, complete with two foci  -- or whatever you want to call it.

Mind blowing.

85D  One of the Five Pillars of Islam, referring to prayer

My daughter and son-in-law are fluent in Arabic.  She told me it was salah, which is singular.  However, the answer is salat, which is plural. Then she said it was plural because Muslims pray five times per day.
i had PILLARS for 56-down and PURIS for 56-across for way too long. this even worked with a lot of the overlapping clues so it was pretty frustrating. very evil misdirection.

What a lovely Sunday grid. Those huge spanner’s DAUNTed me at first, but they filled surprisingly quickly.
I see our bête noire; USvUK linguistic/cultural differences strikes again. As other Brits on here have noted, ‘HAVE IT OUT’ is in common usage here, where it appears ‘hash’ is the operative term across the Pond. A rare instance of the NYT grid chiming with British English without it being stressed in the clue. Happy days.

An enthusiastic singer, can’t quite recall what animal and a jaded Dylanesque Hare producer, sending the singer further and further away to quieten the lyrics. Funny.

Solved the puzzle without assistance in about 45 minutes. Was considerably slowed by holding onto SIDES rather than SODAS and HASHTHINGSOUT rather than HAVETHINGSOUT.

The paired spanners were impressive, as was the central oval. And there were a lot of very nice long entries too. And then we had ODS not clued as a verb, a non-ornithological clue for NENE, "eddies" as a verb (or WHIRLS as a noun?), FTD (maybe this is not as obscure as I think?), FICS, a SILENTA in "diamond" (which for me has a very short but clearly vocalized A), INC and ING, and ISOLDE crossing SALAT!

Add in CIS (which for some reason seems to trigger some commenters) and WARIO (Is this too soon?) and ... well the comments should be a lot of fun today.

While I miss the humor that usually accompanies the Sunday puzzle, this one made up for it with exceptional fill.
Themeless Sunday puzzle completed under protest. 🙂
Fantastic puzzle! So many long stacked clues with so few black squares = superhuman feat of crossword construction.

If I had had 100 guesses to guess who the constructor was, I wouldn't have picked Erik Agard.  No awful pop culture trivia to wade through.  Cluing that I mostly found easy.  And no theme.  But that center oval looks like a swimming pool and the title is FREESTYLE EXERCISE, freestyle being a swimming stroke, and the first long answer is COME ON IN THE WATER'S FINE (which I loved) and there's MOVES AS ONE (water ballet?) and there's a POOL near the bottom -- so my question is did this start out to be a swimming pool puzzle and then was the theme eventually abandoned?  Whatever.  It's by far the most enjoyable Agard puzzle I've ever done, with colorful fill like TONGUE LASHING and LOT IN LIFE and HONEST ANSWER and the fabulous clue for MOLASSES (54D).  There was no suffering at all: it was easy without being obvious or boring.  Loved it!

The clue to 62A does not describe an ironic situation.

The clue for INVERTED ROLLERCOASTER is correct but the explanation and photo choice here in the article are not. The term does not refer to just any roller coaster that has inversions (goes upside down). It is a type where the train rides below the track, and riders' legs hang down like a ski lift. Patriot at Worlds of Fun in the constructor's home town is a prime example.

What a fun (and challenging) puzzle! According to my statistics, it's the 700th NYT crossword I've solved, which I managed in about 8 minutes under my Sunday average. I had no idea I've solved so many, and the time was surprising, because I thought this one was extremely tricky (but fair)!

My favorite clue was 58A, which brought back really fond memories of watching 007 movies with my dad. 🕵️‍♂️📽️

This was a very satisfying solve. I loved watching apparently impenetrable answers fall each time I made another pass through the grid. It was kind of a twofer because after the enjoyment of the 2-coffee solve, there was the different enjoyment of just gawking at the construction.
FAB Sunday!  Honey boo-boo made me laugh. Thanks for a delightful puzzle, Erik!

The middle section had so many INGs in a diagonal line that I thought I'd stumbled on a theme. HAVETHINGSOUT, not being a phrase anyone would actually say, also really tied up the area making this a tough but still enjoyable solve.

Ods bodkins! A Sunday themeless puzzle? That's a choice, I guess. I prefer having a theme to chivvy me along and keep me interested for an hour, but that's just, like, my opinion, man.

"Honey boo-boo" as a clue made me laugh, but if a honeybee stings you, their stinger falls off, and they die, so that's best avoided. Our neighbor in Maryland kept bees, so our flowers were always nicely pollinated, and the occasional jar of fresh honey was wonderful. Never once got stung, BTW.

I like it when A.I. agrees with me:

No, the letter "a" is not silent in "diamond." Most speakers pronounce it as a soft "uh" sound ("dy-uh-mund"). In fast speech, the sound is sometimes skipped ("dy-mund"). 
Pronunciation of Diamond
Normal Speech: Pronounced with a short, weak vowel sound in the middle.
Fast Speech: The middle sound disappears completely in casual talk.

If the clue is [Dutch city with a namesake jar] it's spelled Leyden and not Leiden. Also, if we are expected to honor scientific jargon, [Gene-activating substance] might be any number of molecules or proteins. From Google/AI:

“Genes are activated when specialized proteins called transcription factors attach to specific DNA regions, unwinding the tight physical structure of the genetic material so that an enzyme named RNA polymerase can copy the gene into messenger RNA.”

“Inducer” is a hopelessly vague answer - painfully similar-sounding to the now ubiquitous "influencer".

Two moments can affect your streak: when you start a puzzle and when you solve a puzzle. 
My experience is that your streak continues for at least another 24 hours (i.e., one day's grace) after the puzzle drops PROVIDED you don't open any following puzzle. A linguistics teacher once taught us that when asked to report how they speak, people often default to how they think it's supposed to be pronounced or said.  But they don't actually speak that way.
